title: Use animal handling and protection equipment

lessons.title: Handling equipment and emergency euthanasia equipment
lessons.html:
Animal handling equipment

Animal welfare workers and farm staff use equipment to catch, hold and move animals safely. The right tool, used correctly, protects both the animal and the handler.

EquipmentUse
Leash, slip lead, harnessLeading and controlling dogs
Muzzle (basket or fabric)Preventing bites during examination; basket muzzles let the dog pant
Catch pole (control pole)Holding an aggressive or unsocialised dog at a distance; the loop goes over the head and one front leg where possible, never tightened to choke
Cat grasper, cat trap, crush cageCatching feral or frightened cats and giving injections safely
Thick gloves, towels, blanketsHandling cats, small animals and birds
Halters, lead ropesHorses, donkeys and cattle
Crush, head clamp, raceRestraining cattle for treatment
Snake tongs and hooksMoving snakes, by trained people only

Choose the least stressful method that is still safe. A friendly dog needs only a leash; a frightened dog in a corner may need a catch pole. Never drag an animal by a catch pole or use it to lift an animal off the ground.

Emergency euthanasia equipment

When an animal is badly injured, for example a horse hit by a car or a cow trapped in a ditch, emergency euthanasia may be needed. The common tools are:

  • Firearms of the correct calibre for the species, used by a licensed and trained person.
  • Captive bolt pistol (penetrating), followed at once by bleeding or pithing.
  • Injectable euthanasia drugs, used only by or under the direct control of a veterinarian.

Such equipment must be locked away when not in use, cartridges for captive bolts must match the species, and firearm laws must be followed. Hands-on training is essential before anyone uses this equipment.

lessons.title: Temporary barriers, traffic equipment, maintenance and records
lessons.html:
Temporary containment barriers

At an accident scene, a stray livestock call or a rescue, you often need to contain animals quickly. Useful barriers include:

  • Portable panels or hurdles that clip together to form a pen.
  • Rolls of mesh or snow fencing with steel droppers.
  • Rope and tape lines with flags to guide animals.
  • Your vehicle and trailer, parked to block an escape route.
  • Sheets of board held by helpers to guide pigs or sheep.

Barriers must be high and strong enough for the species, with no gaps or sharp ends. Do not pen animals in a way that traps people with them.

Traffic equipment

Animals on roads cause serious accidents. When working at a roadside:

  • Park safely off the road with hazard lights and the amber light bar on.
  • Wear a reflective bib.
  • Place warning triangles or cones well before the scene in both directions.
  • Ask the police or traffic officers to control traffic where possible.
  • Never stand between an animal and oncoming traffic.

Maintenance of equipment

  • Clean and disinfect leashes, muzzles, catch poles and cages after each use to prevent spread of diseases such as parvovirus.
  • Check catch-pole cables and locking mechanisms, cage doors and trap triggers for wear.
  • Clean and service captive bolt pistols as the manufacturer instructs; store cartridges dry.
  • Replace frayed ropes and cracked muzzles immediately.

The need for records

Records show that equipment is safe and used responsibly. Keep:

  • A maintenance log for each item: date checked, fault found, repair done, by whom.
  • A firearm and ammunition register, as required by firearm law.
  • A register of scheduled drugs, kept by the vet.
  • A record of each euthanasia: animal, reason, method, person, date.

Good records protect staff if a case goes to court and help managers plan replacements.

Key points

  • Pick the least stressful safe tool: leash, muzzle, catch pole, cat grasper or crush.
  • Emergency euthanasia equipment includes firearms, captive bolts and vet-only drugs.
  • Use portable panels, mesh and vehicles as temporary barriers.
  • At roadsides, use hazard lights, reflective bibs and triangles.
  • Clean, check and log all equipment, and keep firearm and euthanasia records.
